evidence: src/infrastructure/UserController.ts: `private userRepository: IUserRepository;` is stored next to `createUserUseCase`, and GET /users calls `this.userRepository.findAll().map((user) => ({ id: user.getId(), name: user.getName() }))` without going through any use case.

src/infrastructure/ProjectController.ts and src/infrastructure/TaskController.ts send every route through a use case (`createProjectUseCase.execute`, `createTaskUseCase.execute`, `listTasksUseCase.execute`, `assignTaskUseCase.execute`, `markTaskDoneUseCase.execute`) and pass the result to `res.json(...)` unchanged.

The same catch block, `const message = error instanceof Error ? error.message : "Unknown error"; res.status(400).json({ error: message });`, appears in ProjectController.ts (1 time), TaskController.ts (4 times) and UserController.ts (1 time).
ProjectController.ts and UserController.ts both contain `if (!name) { res.status(400).json({ error: "Name is required" }); return; }`.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: The module has one concern: the HTTP adapter (controllers), the in-memory repositories, and the composition root (app.ts, server.ts). The controllers set a clear pattern: each route calls an application use case built in the constructor. UserController breaks that pattern on GET /users. It keeps its own userRepository field, calls userRepository.findAll() directly with no use case, and builds the response shape ({id, name}) by hand. Every other route returns the use-case result as-is, so this is a bypass of the module's own abstraction, and the way responses are serialized is inconsistent. One error-handling rule is also copied into every handler in all three controllers instead of living in one place: catch the error, read error.message or fall back to "Unknown error", and reply 400. The "Name is required" check is also duplicated between ProjectController and UserController.
